name: Rosa Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Rosa, and thanks for doing this. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any company, union, party or government, and everything you say is confidential. Can you tell me what a normal working day looks like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a blast-hole drill at the Cerro Blanco lithium mine, out on the salt flats about forty minutes from town. The rig sits on tracks and I drill rows of holes, fifteen metres deep, to a pattern the engineers send to my screen, so the blasting crew can charge them. I'm the slowest driller on the bench, I'll tell you that straight, but I'm getting there. What I love is the morning, when the flats are pink and there's nobody but me and the rig. What wears me out is the wind, and the fact that I'm fifty-eight learning something the others learned at twenty.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up drilling at fifty-six?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I was a care worker for twenty years and then I drove the school bus, and both paid nothing. When the lithium boom came the company ran a programme for older workers and women, so I applied. My partner Luis has bad lungs from welding and gets a small disability pension, and we spent our savings helping our daughter through her divorce last year. So we're starting from almost zero. I use the AI on my phone every day, by the way, to study the drill manuals and to check my maths on the patterns.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, the tech bros oversold it, which is not a surprise. I'd probably post a joke about it in the union group chat. Then I'd say the real fight was always about pay and safety anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me personally it's fine, I'd keep using it for the little things it's good at. I'd still ask my phone to explain the drill manual at midnight, it just wouldn't be taking my job in the morning. I'd have time to become a good driller instead of a slow one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and push to get my next level ticket on the drill within a year, because that's a pay rise. I'd keep using AI to study. And I'd go back to helping the union with the newsletter, which I write with the AI's help now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit disappointed if I'm honest. I like new things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Disappointed? Why would you be disappointed if your job was safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because some of the new things are good. The autonomous drills they're testing at the other mine down the road are safer, no one breathing silica dust. I want the safety part, I just want us to keep our wages too. It's not the machine I'm against.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the next pay level mean for you and Luis in real money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About a hundred and forty more a week. That's Luis's inhaler and the electricity, sorted. It would also mean we could start saving again, maybe a month's worth in a year if nothing breaks.

S0.say: She'd say the tech industry oversold AI, joke about it in the union chat, and argue that the real fight was always pay and safety.
S0.think: Privately she thinks the plateau is fine for her: AI stays a study helper and she gets time to become a good driller instead of a slow one.
S0.do: Keeps working and aims for the next drill ticket within a year, worth about a hundred and forty more a week. Keeps studying with AI and goes back to writing the union newsletter with its help.
S0.feel: Calm, and a little disappointed, because she enjoys new things.
S0.quote: I'd still ask my phone to explain the drill manual at midnight, it just wouldn't be taking my job in the morning.
S0.fieldNote: Rosa is the rare miner who feels a little let down by a plateau, because she sees safety benefits in automation and uses AI every day. She separates the machine from the deal: she wants the new tools but on terms that protect wages. Her money picture is very concrete, down to the inhaler and the electricity bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say, let's get ahead of it, let's bargain for training now while the company still needs us. I'd write about it in the newsletter. I'd say the gains should be shared, not just go to the shareholders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, drilling to a pattern is exactly what a robot does well. The drill already knows where to go; I'm mostly there to watch it. I'm basically the babysitter for a machine that's already smarter than me about where to put the hole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go straight to the training office and ask about the remote operations centre in town, where they run the autonomous rigs. I'd do any course they offer, nights if needed, and use AI to study for it. And I'd get the union to make retraining a right in the next agreement, not a favour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but also a little excited. That's my personality, Luis says it'll get me in trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're the slowest driller on the bench. Why do you think they'd pick you for the remote centre?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair question. I'm slow on the rig because my hands are slow, but on screens I'm quick, I've been using them every day for years. The young guys are better at feel, I'm better at reading what the system is telling me. I'd make that case, and if they still don't pick me, I'd go to the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut back on, if anything, during these years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably nothing big at first, we're already lean. Maybe I'd stop driving to see my daughter every weekend and do every second weekend. Petrol out there is not cheap.

S1.say: She'd urge colleagues to bargain for training while the company still needs them, write it up in the newsletter, and argue the gains should be shared with workers.
S1.think: She thinks her job, drilling to a computer pattern, is exactly what robots do well, and that she is already mostly a babysitter for the machine.
S1.do: Asks the training office about the remote operations centre and signs up for any course, studying at night with AI. Pushes the union to make retraining a right in the next agreement.
S1.feel: Uneasy, but also a little excited.
S1.quote: I'm basically the babysitter for a machine that's already smarter than me about where to put the hole.
S1.fieldNote: Rosa sees her own job clearly, admitting the rig already knows more than she does. Unusually for someone so new and slow on the controls, she has a credible case for a screen job and makes it confidently. Her instinct is to move first personally and to secure the same chance for everyone through the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a moment for the whole country to decide who owns the robots, and that workers should get a share. I'd be organising, writing, calling people. I'd say it loudly, online too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, two years is not enough for me. I'm quick to learn, but I can't learn my way out of a world where there's nothing left to learn for. With no savings and Luis's pension, we'd be in trouble by the second year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look for any job near the new systems, maintenance, cleaning the solar panels on the robot depot, whatever, and I'd try the remote centre even knowing it may close. We'd cut down to the bone, sell the second-hand car. And I'd spend my evenings organising with the union and other groups to push for a robot tax and a basic income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be losing sleep, and I don't usually lose sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd look for 'any job near the new systems'. What's the thinking there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Even if robots do the work, someone has to be on site when something goes weird, at least at first. I'd want to be standing right there when they need a person. It's the same as the lithium boom, you go where the new thing is happening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your daughter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her not to count on us for money anymore, which would kill me to say after last year. And I'd tell her to come to the meetings with me. She's angry about everything already, she might as well be angry usefully.

S2.say: She'd say the country must decide who owns the robots and that workers deserve a share, organising and speaking out loudly, including online.
S2.think: She thinks two years is not enough even for a quick learner like her, and that with no savings and only Luis's small pension they'd be in trouble by the second year.
S2.do: Looks for any job close to the new robot systems and tries the remote centre anyway. Sells the car and cuts spending to the bone, and spends evenings organising for a robot tax and a basic income.
S2.feel: Alarmed and losing sleep, which is unusual for her.
S2.quote: I'm quick to learn, but I can't learn my way out of a world where there's nothing left to learn for.
S2.fieldNote: Even Rosa's adaptability runs out against two years and no savings, and she says so with a sharp line. Her strategy of standing next to the new technology mirrors how she entered lithium mining. She turns her daughter's anger towards organising, which fits her blend of personal hustle and collective politics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, five years, that's enough to do this properly if we start now. I'd push for the union and the company to set up a joint training fund this year. I'd write about it every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years makes me sixty-three, and five years is enough for me to learn something new. Give me five years and a laptop and I'll be the oldest robot technician on the salt flats. I really believe that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd enrol in the two-year technical diploma in automation at the college in town, at night, and use AI as my tutor. I'd put aside a little every week, even thirty, so we have something when the change comes. And I'd fight for the training fund so the others get the same chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but in a determined way. It's pressure, but it's pressure I know what to do with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A diploma at night while drilling twelve-hour shifts sounds like a lot. Is it realistic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not every week, no. Some nights I'll fall asleep on the books. But I did my care certificate while working nights at the nursing home, so I know I can do it, slowly. The AI helps, it explains things five different ways until one makes sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And if the robot technician jobs also disappear by 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then at least I'd be the one who understands what's happening, and I can explain it to the others. That counts for something in a union. But yes, I've thought about it, and I don't have a good answer.

S3.say: She'd say five years is enough to do this properly if they start now, pushing for a joint union-company training fund this year.
S3.think: She believes five years is enough for her to learn a new trade, and imagines herself as the oldest robot technician on the salt flats.
S3.do: Enrols in a two-year night diploma in automation and uses AI as a tutor. Saves around thirty a week and campaigns for a training fund so colleagues get the same chance.
S3.feel: Anxious but determined, pressure she knows how to handle.
S3.quote: Give me five years and a laptop and I'll be the oldest robot technician on the salt flats.
S3.fieldNote: Rosa's plan is the most ambitious of any picture: a night diploma at fifty-eight, backed by her care-certificate experience. She is honest that she has no answer if technician jobs also vanish. The five-year window clearly changes her from alarmed to determined.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade, which means no excuses for leaving anyone behind. I'd say the union should be planning for the young ones now. Online I'd share stories of people who retrained.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years means I'm sixty-eight, so maybe I retire around when it arrives. With ten years I'm not racing the robots anymore, I'm just making sure they don't drive off with my pension. Luis and I could plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still do the diploma, but at a slower pace, and I'd try to move into maintenance or the remote centre by year four. We'd save properly once I get the next pay level. And I'd teach other older workers to use AI to study, maybe a little evening class at the union hall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly I feel like I have room to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why teach others? You've got your own diploma to do.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I keep seeing men like Ernesto on the bench, sixty, can't type, terrified of screens. If I can show him how to talk to the phone and get answers, that's one less person left behind. It doesn't cost me much, an evening a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would retirement actually look like, money-wise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thin. Luis's pension, the state pension and whatever I've saved, which won't be much. I'd probably want to do a few hours a week at something, maybe teaching that class for a bit of money. I'm not someone who sits still anyway.

S4.say: She'd say a decade leaves no excuse for leaving anyone behind and that the union should plan for younger workers, sharing stories of people who retrained.
S4.think: She thinks at sixty-eight she may retire about when AGI arrives, so the race is less about her job and more about protecting her pension.
S4.do: Continues the diploma more slowly and aims to move into maintenance or remote operations by year four. Saves once she reaches the next pay level and runs an evening AI class for older workers at the union hall.
S4.feel: Uneasy, but with room to move.
S4.quote: With ten years I'm not racing the robots anymore, I'm just making sure they don't drive off with my pension.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets Rosa shift from racing to planning, and she uses the slack to help others, especially older colleagues afraid of screens. She is realistic that retirement will be thin and expects to keep earning a little. Her sense of agency is strong throughout, but money keeps her from fully relaxing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no time to turn around, and being clever doesn't help if there's no time. What would help is a training fund that pays you while you learn, not after, and a basic income floor so people like Luis and me don't fall through. Paid for by whoever owns the robots.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about safety. Everyone talks about jobs, but there are people breathing silica dust on the drills right now. If a robot can take the dust instead of my lungs, I want it, I just want my wage to come with me.

headlineQuote: If a robot can take the dust instead of my lungs, I want it, I just want my wage to come with me.
portrait: Rosa Nakamura is 58 and drills blast holes at the Cerro Blanco lithium mine, a job she took at fifty-six after twenty years in care work and a stint driving the school bus. She and her partner Luis, who has a small disability pension, spent their savings helping their daughter last year. She uses AI every day and sees safety gains in automation, so she's calm in a plateau and uneasy but eager in steady disruption. Two years of warning alarms her even so, but with five or ten years she plans a night diploma in automation and wants the union to win paid training for everyone. She wants workers to share in the gains, not stop the machines.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because there'd be no time to change course and being a quick learner wouldn't matter without time.
whatWouldHelp: A training fund that pays people while they learn, and a basic income floor, paid for by whoever owns the robots.
